implementation_notes: C's premature optimisation has a specific and very common form: replacing a standard-library or well-tested implementation with a hand-written one on the theory that it will be faster, usually with no benchmark at all. The second form is micro-tuning a memory layout — bit-fields, packed structs, manual alignment — before the struct's size has been shown to matter. C also has the sharpest instance of the legitimate case: embedded targets with a hard memory budget, where a smaller data structure is a requirement rather than an optimisation. The counter is cheap here: `-pg` with gprof, `perf stat`, or a micro-benchmark harness.
idiom_name: hand-rolled primitives before a measurement; -O flags as a substitute for profiling
pitfalls: `qsort` replaced by a hand-rolled sort is almost always slower and always less tested.
Bit-packing a struct before measuring whether its size affects anything is the C form of the smell.
Hand-inlining functions based on folklore about call overhead, on platforms where the compiler inlines them anyway.
`-Ofast` changes floating-point semantics; applying it for speed without a numerical requirement is a correctness risk, not an optimisation.
